experiences/aldersgate-heart-strangely-w: Wesley's heart 'strangely warmed' at Aldersgate
Aldersgate Street, London

From John Wesley's Journal, 24 May 1738 (public domain): 'In the evening I went very unwillingly to a society in Aldersgate Street, where one was reading Luther's preface to the Epistle to the Romans. About a quarter before nine, while he was describing the change which God works in the heart through faith in Christ, I felt my heart strangely warmed. I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation; and an assurance was given me that He had taken away my sins, even mine, and saved me from the law of sin and death.' On 1 January 1739, at a Fetter Lane love feast, Wesley records that 'the power of God came mightily upon us', many crying out for joy and falling to the ground.

Wesley, influenced by the Moravian Peter Böhler, interpreted the experience as receiving the assurance of saving faith. His brother Charles had a similar experience three days earlier. In Wesley's field-preaching from 1739, hearers often cried out, convulsed or fell; Wesley generally regarded this as God's work mixed with natural and sometimes diabolical elements.
Methodist

Aldersgate Day (24 May) is commemorated; the experience grounds the Methodist doctrine of assurance, though historians and Methodist theologians debate whether it was Wesley's 'conversion' or one stage in a longer journey.
Anglican
Wesley remained an Anglican priest; contemporary bishops worried about 'enthusiasm' and the irregularity of field-preaching.
Pentecostal / charismatic
Wesley's account of people falling under the power of God is often cited as a historical precedent for being 'slain in the Spirit'.
Historian
Henry Rack shows Wesley's later journals rarely mention Aldersgate and that his spiritual doubts continued; the episode gained iconic status largely in 19th-century Methodism.
Assurance of salvation: normative or occasional?
Was Aldersgate Wesley's conversion?
Enthusiasm and bodily manifestations in early Methodism.

John Wesley was born in 1703 at Epworth, Lincolnshire, the fifteenth child of Samuel Wesley, a High Church Anglican rector, and Susanna Wesley, a strong-minded and devout mother. Rescued as a small child from a fire at the rectory in 1709, he was later described by his mother as a 'brand plucked from the burning'. At Oxford, where he became a fellow of Lincoln College, he and his brother Charles led a small group of earnest students, mocked as the 'Holy Club' and 'Methodists' for their methodical rule of prayer, fasting, frequent communion, Bible study and visits to prisoners.

In October 1735 John and Charles sailed as missionaries to the new colony of Georgia. On the voyage a terrible storm terrified the English passengers, but a group of German Moravians sang psalms calmly throughout. Wesley noted in his journal that he asked one whether he was not afraid and was told no, not even the women and children. In Georgia, the Moravian leader August Gottlieb Spangenberg asked him whether he knew Jesus Christ and had the witness of the Spirit within himself, questions Wesley could answer only uncertainly. His ministry in Savannah was a failure: his strict High Church practice antagonised parishioners, and after a failed romance with Sophia Hopkey and a legal dispute when he refused her communion, he left in December 1737.

Back in England in February 1738, he wrote that he had gone to America to convert the Indians, but who would convert him? He met the young Moravian Peter Böhler, who persuaded him that true faith brings instant forgiveness, assurance and peace, and that he lacked it. Böhler advised him to 'preach faith till you have it; and then, because you have it, you will preach faith'. On Whitsunday, 21 May 1738, Charles, ill in bed, experienced assurance of forgiveness and wrote in his journal of finding peace with God.

Three days later, on Wednesday 24 May 1738, John records that he opened his Bible at five in the morning on the words that he was not far from the kingdom of God, and in the afternoon heard the anthem at St Paul's Cathedral, 'Out of the deep have I called unto thee, O Lord'. His journal continues: "In the evening I went very unwillingly to a society in Aldersgate Street, where one was reading Luther's preface to the Epistle to the Romans. About a quarter before nine, while he was describing the change which God works in the heart through faith in Christ, I felt my heart strangely warmed. I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation; and an assurance was given me that he had taken away my sins, even mine, and saved me from the law of sin and death." He prayed for those who had mistreated him and testified to everyone there, and was then taken by friends to Charles, who greeted him with the hymn he had just written.

Wesley's journal shows that doubts and temptations returned in the following months, and he even wrote at times that he was not a Christian. In the summer of 1738 he visited Herrnhut and met Zinzendorf. On 1 January 1739, at a love feast at the Fetter Lane Society in London with the Wesleys, George Whitefield and others, he reported that about three in the morning the power of God came on them mightily, so that many cried out for joy and fell to the ground. In April 1739, at Whitefield's urging, he overcame his scruples and preached in the open air near Bristol to some three thousand people. From then until his death in 1791 he travelled about 250,000 miles on horseback, preaching perhaps 40,000 sermons and organising converts into societies, classes and bands within the Church of England.

Interpretations of Aldersgate differ. Methodist tradition has often treated it as Wesley's evangelical conversion; others, noting his earlier devotion and later doubts, see it as one stage in a longer process of assurance and a turning point in his preaching. Wesley himself rarely referred to the date afterwards. It is nonetheless commemorated each year by Methodists as 'Aldersgate Day', and a memorial near the site in the City of London marks the event.

Aldersgate became the defining moment in Methodist memory and a classic statement of evangelical assurance of salvation by faith. The movement that followed, Methodism, grew into a worldwide family of churches, gave rise to the Holiness and, indirectly, Pentecostal movements, and helped shape evangelical Christianity and social reform in Britain and America. Wesley's teaching on assurance and Christian perfection was criticised by Calvinists such as Whitefield and by Anglican authorities as 'enthusiasm', and scholars still debate whether Aldersgate was a conversion or one step in a longer journey. It also shows the influence of Luther and the Moravians on English religion.
experiences/cane-ridge-revival/title: Cane Ridge camp meeting: falling, jerks and holy laughter
experiences/cane-ridge-revival/place/nam: Cane Ridge Meeting House, Bourbon County, Kentucky
experiences/cane-ridge-revival/account: Paraphrase of Barton W. Stone's autobiography and contemporary letters: at a Presbyterian sacramental gathering on 6-12 August 1801, attended by an estimated 10,000-20,000 people with Presbyterian, Methodist and Baptist preachers speaking from several stands at once, many fell to the ground and lay helpless for hours. Stone lists 'exercises': the falling exercise, the jerks (violent jerking of head and body), the dancing, barking, laughing, running and singing exercises.
experiences/cane-ridge-revival/contempor: Supporters saw an American Pentecost; critics in the Presbyterian Synod of Kentucky saw disorder and doctrinal laxity. The revival contributed to the Cumberland Presbyterian and Stone-Campbell (Christian Church/Disciples) splits and fuelled the Methodist and Baptist camp-meeting tradition.
experiences/cane-ridge-revival/assessmen: Remembered as a foundational frontier revival; Stone himself later grew more cautious, judging some exercises genuine and others the result of excitement or imitation.
Often regarded as an example of revivalism that confused emotion with grace and weakened confessional order.
Cited as a precedent for falling, shaking and laughter in modern revivals such as Toronto (1994).

Paul Conkin calls it 'America's Pentecost'; historians emphasise sacramental-season roots in Scottish Presbyterianism, crowd dynamics and frontier social life; Ann Taves traces how such 'fits and trances' were interpreted religiously and medically.
experiences/cane-ridge-revival/story:
At the end of the eighteenth century Kentucky was a raw frontier, admitted as a state only in 1792. Settlers from Virginia, the Carolinas and Pennsylvania lived scattered across the countryside with few churches, and ministers complained of irreligion, drunkenness and violence. Presbyterians, many of Scots-Irish background, kept the old Scottish custom of 'sacramental seasons' or 'holy fairs': multi-day communion gatherings with preaching, fasting, self-examination and the Lord's Supper, which in Scotland had sometimes become occasions of revival.

In 1800 James McGready, a Presbyterian minister in Logan County in south-western Kentucky, led communion seasons at the Red River and Gasper River meeting houses where people fell to the ground, cried out and professed conversion. Because people came from long distances and camped on the grounds in wagons and tents, these gatherings became known as camp meetings. In the spring of 1801 Barton W. Stone, the young Presbyterian pastor of the Cane Ridge and Concord congregations in Bourbon County, near Paris in central Kentucky, travelled to Logan County to see the revivals for himself and returned deeply impressed. Revival spread through central Kentucky that summer.

Stone arranged a communion season at the Cane Ridge meeting house, a log church built in 1791, beginning on Friday 6 August 1801. Contemporary estimates of the crowd ranged from about 10,000 to 25,000 people, at a time when the largest town in the state, Lexington, had fewer than 2,000 inhabitants. Presbyterian, Methodist and some Baptist ministers preached simultaneously from stands and wagons in different parts of the grounds, day and night, for about six days. Over a thousand people are said to have received communion.

Eyewitnesses, including Stone himself in his later autobiography and several letters published at the time, described extraordinary bodily 'exercises'. People fell to the ground, sometimes lying unconscious for hours: the 'falling exercise'. Others experienced 'the jerks', violent involuntary twitching of the head and body; some danced, ran, laughed uncontrollably or, according to some reports, made barking sounds. Many cried out for mercy and then shouted for joy at conversion. One Presbyterian minister estimated that some three thousand people fell during the meeting. Critics also reported drinking, disorder and sexual misbehaviour on the fringes of the encampment, though defenders thought such reports exaggerated.

Reactions were sharply divided. Supporters saw the meeting as an outpouring of the Holy Spirit comparable to Pentecost. Many Presbyterian leaders were alarmed by the disorder, by the cooperation with Methodists and by the revivalists' tendency to downplay Calvinist doctrines of predestination in favour of a universal call to repent. In 1803 Stone and four other ministers withdrew from the Synod of Kentucky and formed the independent Springfield Presbytery; in June 1804 they dissolved it in a document called 'The Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery', resolving to be simply 'Christians' guided by the Bible alone. Two of them, Richard McNemar and John Dunlavy, soon joined the Shakers. In south-western Kentucky, disputes over licensing revival preachers without the usual education led to the formation of the Cumberland Presbyterian Church in 1810.

Methodists, especially under bishop Francis Asbury, adopted the camp meeting enthusiastically, and it became a standard feature of American frontier religion for much of the nineteenth century. Stone's 'Christians' joined with the followers of Alexander Campbell in 1832, forming the core of the Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement, from which the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), the Churches of Christ and the independent Christian Churches descend. The Cane Ridge meeting house still stands, now protected by a stone superstructure, as a shrine of that movement.

experiences/cane-ridge-revival/significa: Cane Ridge is often called 'America's Pentecost' and was a high point of the Second Great Awakening on the frontier, popularising the camp meeting as a vehicle for mass revival, especially among Methodists and Baptists. It reshaped American Protestantism by encouraging a more democratic, experiential and Arminian-leaning religion, and it directly contributed to the Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement and the Cumberland Presbyterians. Its bodily manifestations prefigured debates about revival phenomena that recur in Holiness, Pentecostal and charismatic movements. Critics, then and now, questioned its emotionalism and disorder, and historians analyse it as a product of frontier social conditions as well as religious fervour.
